summary:
The Wealden iron industry, based in south-eastern England, became one of Britain’s major iron-producing regions. It relied on ironstone found in the Weald’s clay beds and charcoal made from local woodland. Water power later drove blast-furnace bellows and forge hammers, requiring networks of ponds and dams.

Ironmaking took place in the region before the Roman conquest, expanded greatly under Roman rule, and then largely disappeared after the Romans left. It revived in the ninth century using bloomery technology, and water-powered bloomeries appeared from about the 14th century. Blast furnaces and finery forges, introduced around 1490, transformed production: nearly 180 sites operated over the following centuries.

The industry reached its height in the late 16th century, producing more than 9,000 tons of iron annually in the 1590s and supplying London and the armaments trade. Weald ironworkers began casting cannon in 1543, and cannon production remained important until after the Seven Years’ War. The region also produced notable cast-iron railings for St Paul’s Cathedral in the early 18th century.

From the 17th century, Wealden bar iron faced competition from Midland and imported Swedish iron. The wider industry eventually declined because it depended on charcoal and had no accessible coal to fuel coke-fired furnaces. Most works closed by the late 18th century, though ponds, dams and other traces of the industry remain across the Weald.
unsupportedClaims: Water-powered blast furnaces and forges required networks of ponds and dams. The points say that a series of ponds often supplied a furnace waterwheel, not that such networks were required.
Ironmaking expanded greatly under Roman rule. The points establish substantial Roman production but do not quantify growth from pre-Roman levels.
Cannon production remained important until after the Seven Years’ War. The points say it remained a major activity until the end of the war.
The Weald definitely made the St Paul’s Cathedral railings. The points say that Lamberhurst Foundry is believed to have made them.
Most works closed by the late 18th century. The points do not give a deadline by which most works had closed.
